entries.text_en: The Stretched Rohini Satellite Series (SROSS) represents a pioneering chapter in India’s space exploration history, developed by the Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO) as successors to the earlier Rohini satellites. Launched between 1987 and 1994, these small scientific satellites were designed to conduct astrophysics experiments, Earth remote sensing, and upper atmospheric monitoring. The series also served as testbeds for novel mission concepts, pushing the boundaries of what India could achieve in low-Earth orbit. A key highlight of the SROSS program was its role as the payload for the developmental flights of the Augmented Satellite Launch Vehicle (ASLV), a precursor to India’s more advanced launch systems like the PSLV. Despite early setbacks—including two failed launches due to ASLV’s maiden flight issues—the program ultimately succeeded in deploying two operational satellites (SROSS-C and SROSS-D) that carried gamma-ray burst detectors and atmospheric instruments, contributing valuable data to global astrophysics and meteorology research. The SROSS series exemplified India’s resilience in space technology, blending ambition with incremental progress during a transformative era for the country’s space agency.
